text: Early the next morning all the chief priests and elders of the people met to decide how to put Jesus to death.
They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate, the Roman governor.
When Judas, who had betrayed him, saw that Jesus had been condemned, he was filled with remorse and returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders.
"I've sinned," he said, "I've betrayed innocent blood." "What's that to us?" they replied. "That's your problem."
So Judas threw the silver into the temple, left, and went and hanged himself.
The chief priests picked up the coins and said, "It's not lawful to put this in the treasury, since it's blood money."
So they decided to use it to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners.
That's why the field is still called the Field of Blood today.
This fulfilled what the prophet had spoken: they took the thirty silver coins, the price set on him by the people of Israel,
and used them for the potter's field, just as the Lord had directed.
Jesus now stood before the governor, who asked him, "Are you the king of the Jews?" "You say so," Jesus answered.
But when the chief priests and elders brought accusations against him, he gave no answer.
"Don't you hear all the charges against you?" Pilate asked.
But Jesus wouldn't answer even one charge, and the governor was greatly amazed.
Now it was the governor's custom at the festival to release one prisoner the crowd chose.
At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner named Barabbas.
So when the crowd gathered, Pilate asked, "Which one do you want me to release — Barabbas, or Jesus who is called the Messiah?"
He knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over.
While Pilate was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word: "Have nothing to do with that innocent man — I've suffered greatly today in a dream because of him."
But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus executed.
"Which of the two do you want me to release?" the governor asked. "Barabbas," they answered.
"Then what should I do with Jesus who is called the Messiah?" Pilate asked. They all said, "Crucify him!"
"Why? What crime has he committed?" But they shouted all the louder, "Crucify him!"
Seeing he was getting nowhere, and that a riot was starting, Pilate took water and washed his hands before the crowd. "I'm innocent of this man's blood," he said. "It's on you."
All the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
Then he released Barabbas to them, but had Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified.
The governor's soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole company around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on his head, and put a reed in his right hand. Then they knelt and mocked him: "Hail, king of the Jews!"
They spat on him, took the reed, and struck him on the head with it.
After mocking him, they took off the robe, put his own clothes back on him, and led him away to crucify him.
On the way out they found a man from Cyrene named Simon and forced him to carry the cross.
They came to a place called Golgotha, meaning Place of a Skull.
They offered him wine mixed with gall to drink; after tasting it, he refused it.
When they had crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by casting lots.
Then they sat down there to keep watch over him.
Above his head they placed a written charge: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Two rebels were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.
Those who passed by hurled insults, shaking their heads
and saying, "You who were going to tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you're the Son of God, come down from the cross."
The chief priests, scribes, and elders mocked him the same way:
"He saved others; he can't save himself. He's the king of Israel — let him come down from the cross now, and we'll believe him.
He trusted in God; let God rescue him now if he wants him, since he said, I am the Son of God."
The two rebels crucified with him hurled the same insults.
From noon until three in the afternoon, darkness fell over the whole land.
About three, Jesus cried out loudly, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" — meaning, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
Some standing there heard it and said, "He's calling for Elijah."
One of them ran and got a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink.
The rest said, "Leave him — let's see if Elijah comes to save him."
Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The earth shook, and the rocks split.
Tombs broke open, and many bodies of the sleeping holy ones were raised.
They came out of the tombs after his resurrection, entered the holy city, and appeared to many.
When the centurion and those with him keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and everything that happened, they were terrified and said, "Truly this was the Son of God!"
Many women were watching from a distance, the same ones who had followed Jesus from Galilee to care for him.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee's sons.
As evening came, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who was himself a disciple of Jesus, arrived.
He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus' body, and Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
and laid it in his own new tomb, cut into the rock. He rolled a great stone across the entrance and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there, facing the tomb.
The next day, after Preparation Day, the chief priests and Pharisees went together to Pilate
and said, "Sir, we remember that while he was still alive, that deceiver said, After three days I'll rise again.
So give orders to secure the tomb until the third day, or his disciples may come, steal the body, and tell the people he's risen from the dead — and the last deception will be worse than the first."
"You have a guard," Pilate told them. "Go, secure it as best you can."
So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone and posting the guard.
